metadata.title: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative
metadata.method: Transcribed from the user-supplied recording. Shared cases and original question numbers are retained. OCR artifacts are corrected against the frames. Study answers and explanations are independently assessed against ORNAC 17th edition and named clinical references; they are not represented as an official CNA or Meazure answer key.

questions.prompt: Donna is performing an initial count with the scrub nurse. What items does she need to count?
options: Sponges, sharps and miscellaneous items
Sharps and miscellaneous items
Sponges, sharps, instruments and miscellaneous items
Sponges, sharps and instruments
questions.explanation: An initial surgical count accounts for sponges, sharps, instruments, and miscellaneous countable items; minimally invasive access does not remove retained-item risk.
optionExplanations: Omits instruments.
Omits sponges and instruments.
Includes all four count categories.
Omits miscellaneous countable items.

questions.prompt: When setting up the table, the scrub nurse states that she does not need a needle counter for the laparoscopic appendectomy; she only has one needle and one blade on the table. What should the circulating nurse do?
options: Agree with her because cost containment is important.
Give her a needle counter and remind her that safety is for all staff.
Tell the scrub nurse that she will give her one if the case becomes more involved.
Agree because a needle counter is not necessary for only two sharps.
questions.explanation: Contain and track sharps safely even when only a few are used. A small case still exposes personnel to a sharps injury.
optionExplanations: Cost containment cannot justify removing a safety control.
Provides safe sharps containment from the start.
Delays protection until after exposure has already occurred.
Two sharps still require safe containment and counting.

questions.prompt: When entering the abdomen with the trocar, the surgeon has difficulty getting through the peritoneum. Once inside and exploring with the laparoscope, the surgeon notices a perforation in the bowel, and there is leakage. What should the scrub nurse anticipate?
options: Bowel resection
Perforated appendix
Repair of perforated bowel
Gastric ulcer perforation
questions.explanation: The observed problem is an iatrogenic bowel perforation. Prepare for repair and possible conversion to open surgery; resection depends on the extent of injury.
optionExplanations: Resection may be needed for a major injury, but is not established by this description.
The visible injury occurred during trocar entry rather than being described as appendiceal perforation.
Directly addresses the observed bowel injury.
No gastric injury is described.

questions.prompt: The surgical procedure was completed faster than anticipated by the anesthesia provider and Nina is not reversing from the non-depolarizing muscle relaxants given. Which drug is the anesthesia provider likely to give?
options: Succinylcholine chloride (Anectine)
Propofol (Diprivan)
Rocuronium bromide (Zemuron)
Neostigmine bromide (Prostigmin)
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is the listed reversal drug for nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade. Quantitative monitoring and appropriate recovery are needed. The recording names a bromide product; IV reversal uses the prescribed injectable formulation, commonly neostigmine methylsulfate, not an interchangeable salt or route.
optionExplanations: Produces depolarizing neuromuscular blockade rather than reversing it.
Provides hypnosis; it does not reverse paralysis.
Is itself a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker.
The drug class fits reversal, with formulation, monitoring, and antimuscarinic precautions verified.

questions.prompt: Following extubation, Nina’s airway becomes irritated and she shows signs of laryngospasm. What should the circulating nurse anticipate as an initial measure?
options: Administration of succinylcholine chloride (Anectine)
Use a reversal agent for the non-depolarizing muscle relaxant
Provide 100% oxygen using positive pressure delivery
Putting Nina back into an anesthetized state
questions.explanation: Support oxygenation immediately with 100% oxygen, a tight mask, appropriate positive pressure, and jaw thrust while the anesthesia provider removes the stimulus. Persistent spasm may require deepening anesthesia or neuromuscular blockade.
optionExplanations: Can be needed for persistent spasm, but oxygenation measures come first.
Residual paralysis and laryngospasm are different problems.
Addresses the immediate oxygenation problem.
May be part of treatment, but does not replace the initial oxygenation measures.

questions.prompt: The perioperative nurse is transferring Nina to the post-anesthesia care unit. What priorities should be included in the report to the recovery nurse?
options: Drains, Foley catheter, dressing applied
Age, weight, diagnosis, allergies
Allergies, operative procedure performed, laryngospasm
Allergies, location of mother, dressing applied
questions.explanation: Handoff must include the procedure, allergies, and the airway complication so PACU can anticipate recurrent obstruction or other respiratory concerns.
optionExplanations: Useful device and wound details, but omits the described airway event.
Basic assessment details, but omits the significant intraoperative complication.
Conveys the critical event and relevant operative history.
Family location and dressing details do not replace the airway handoff.

questions.prompt: What are the most important things for the circulating nurse to do when she meets Mrs. Snider in the holding area?
options: Confirm the patient's name using a minimum of two patient unique identifiers, confirm consent, and surgical site with patient.
Acknowledge the patient, confirm patient identity with the chart and documents and confirm surgical site accuracy.
Review history and physical examination, confirm consent and check blood results.
Ensure jewellery is removed, check patient health record and confirm n.p.o. status.
questions.explanation: Verify two patient identifiers and reconcile consent, planned procedure, and site with the patient whenever possible before proceeding.
optionExplanations: Includes the essential identity, consent, and site checks.
Does not explicitly reconcile consent with the patient using two identifiers.
Important assessment information, but identity and site verification are still required.
These preparations do not establish the correct patient, consent, and site.

questions.prompt: After Mrs. Snider is positioned and prepped, the scrub nurse is setting up and notices a small tear in the back table cover drape. What should the scrub nurse do?
options: Inform the circulating nurse, dismantle the set-up and order new supplies.
Use a sterile, impervious drape to cover the hole.
Continue with the set-up because Mrs. Snider is already asleep.
Tell the circulating nurse to document the break in technique.
questions.explanation: The tear is a barrier breach requiring immediate assessment and correction. The recording gives no official key and does not state its location, whether contents were exposed, or whether local policy permits controlled over-draping. Replace affected supplies if contamination cannot be excluded; a cover cannot make contaminated items sterile. This item is retained for discussion and is not scored.
optionExplanations: Appropriate when contents are contaminated or contamination cannot be excluded; replacing every item is not necessarily required for every isolated defect.
May be an approved response to an isolated defect only when no contents are contaminated and policy permits it; it cannot reverse existing contamination.
Being anesthetized is not a reason to ignore a barrier breach.
Documenting the event is necessary but does not correct the breach.

questions.prompt: As the surgery progresses, the scrub nurse notices that the incision is larger and more tissue is being dissected than in other segmental resections she has been involved in before. What would be the scrub nurse’s responsibility to the patient?
options: Comment to the surgeon on the extent of the incision.
Bring her concerns to the attention of the circulating nurse.
Ask to see the consent form.
Assume the surgeon knows what he is doing and say nothing.
questions.explanation: Voice the concern to the circulating nurse so the procedure and consent can be reconciled with the surgeon. A larger incision alone does not establish unauthorized surgery.
optionExplanations: A direct safety question may also be useful, but a comment about incision size alone does not reconcile consent.
Initiates coordinated advocacy and verification without assuming wrongdoing.
Obtaining the form alone does not communicate or resolve the concern.
Silence abandons the opportunity to clarify a potentially important discrepancy.

questions.prompt: While Mrs. Snider’s surgery is in progress, several members of the nursing staff visit the operating room to give their best wishes. Since she was already asleep, most hung around the room conversing with the staff and checking periodically on the progress of the surgery. How should the circulating nurse respond to these visitors?
options: Allow only close friends in the operating room.
Send all visitors out of the operating room.
Call the supervisor to restrict traffic flow.
Put a “Closed Room” sign on the door.
questions.explanation: Restrict unnecessary OR traffic and protect the patient's privacy. Staff friendship does not make a social visit part of patient care.
optionExplanations: Friendship does not establish a care-related need to enter.
Removes the unnecessary visitors and restores controlled traffic.
Escalation may follow, but it does not replace the immediate action available to the circulating nurse.
A sign alone does not remove the people already present.

questions.prompt: What should the scrub nurse do first?
options: Ask the circulating nurse to activate the fire alarm.
Attempt to extinguish the flames.
Inform the fire marshal of the incident.
Complete an incident report.
questions.explanation: Protect the patient from the active fire immediately. Alert the team, stop ignition and oxidizer sources through assigned roles, remove burning materials, and extinguish flames with the appropriate method. Reporting follows immediate rescue and control.
optionExplanations: An alarm may be needed, but must not delay immediate protection from flames.
Directly addresses the active fire on the patient and gloves.
Notification is a later reporting step.
Documentation comes after the immediate emergency response.

questions.prompt: How should the perioperative nurse best demonstrate safe electrosurgical practices?
options: By having fire extinguishers readily available in the operating room
By ensuring that the alarm system and audio signal can be turned off
By preventing accidental activation of the active electrode by disconnecting the electrode when not in use
By allowing flammable agents to completely dry before activation of the electrosurgical pencil
questions.explanation: Prevent pooling and allow flammable products to dry completely before draping or activating an ignition source. Drying reduces fuel-related fire risk but does not eliminate every fire-triad hazard.
optionExplanations: Necessary preparedness, but does not directly prevent ignition of the wet agent.
Silencing alerts removes a safety signal.
An insulated holder and safe standby practices matter, but this does not address the wet flammable agent in the case.
Addresses the fuel and ignition interaction illustrated by the case.

questions.prompt: The resident drops the electrosurgical pencil on the floor, and the electrosurgical unit starts to spark. What is the circulating nurse’s most appropriate action?
options: Notify the fire marshal.
Call for help.
Pull the fire alarm.
Unplug the electrosurgical unit.
questions.explanation: Stop using and safely isolate the sparking unit from power if this can be done without contacting damaged wiring or exposing staff to shock. Arrange replacement and biomedical assessment.
optionExplanations: Reporting does not stop the immediate electrical hazard.
Help is appropriate, but isolate the malfunctioning equipment promptly when safe.
An alarm is used when the fire response requires it; it does not isolate the sparking device.
Removes the electrical energy source when safe to do so.

questions.prompt: The surgery is now complete, and final dressings are being applied to the patient. Upon extubation, the patient has difficulty breathing. His colour is dusky and his oxygen saturation is now 79%. What is the circulating nurse’s most appropriate action to assist the anesthesia provider?
options: Call for the crash cart.
Get the difficult airway cart.
Prepare to assist the anesthesia provider with reintubation.
Call for a tracheostomy set.
questions.explanation: Severe post-extubation hypoxemia requires immediate airway and ventilation support. Prepare reintubation equipment and assist the anesthesia provider while oxygenation is addressed.
optionExplanations: May become necessary if arrest occurs, but the described immediate problem is the airway.
Helpful if a difficult airway is anticipated, but directly assisting airway restoration is the listed priority.
Prepares for definitive airway support in the described severe deterioration.
A surgical airway is a rescue pathway, not the first listed response to every post-extubation event.

questions.prompt: The perioperative nurse reviews the consent for surgery form with Chad and his parents. She notices that the consent form indicates ORIF of his right arm rather than his left arm. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse to take?
options: Have Chad sign a new consent indicating the correct side.
Have one of Chad's parents sign a new consent indicating the correct side.
Inform the surgeon and request that he speak with Chad.
Inform the nurse-in-charge and complete an incident report.
questions.explanation: Stop progression until the surgeon clarifies the correct procedure and side with the patient and obtains valid consent. Age alone does not establish incapacity, and recent medication requires assessment rather than assumption.
optionExplanations: A replacement signature alone does not complete the surgeon's consent discussion.
A parent's signature is not automatically the correct solution for every 16-year-old.
Brings the discrepancy to the responsible practitioner for clarification with Chad.
Reporting alone leaves the wrong-side consent unresolved.

questions.prompt: Intraoperatively, the surgeon asks that an additional IV dose of the prophylactic antibiotics be given to Chad. Which of the following antibiotics is most appropriate for this patient?
options: Cefazolin sodium (Kefzol)
Metronidazole (Flagyl)
Vancomycin HCl (Vancocin)
Bacitracin
questions.explanation: The penicillin reaction is unspecified, so a unique antibiotic choice cannot be verified from this stem. Cefazolin is appropriate for many patients with a penicillin allergy label; severe delayed reactions or a confirmed cefazolin allergy require a different assessment and regimen. Vancomycin is not automatically required by any penicillin allergy. Confirm the reaction, previous prophylaxis, timing, and local protocol. This item is not scored.
optionExplanations: Often preferred orthopedic prophylaxis after appropriate allergy assessment; the stem lacks the details needed to exclude it.
Anaerobic coverage alone does not provide standard orthopedic prophylaxis.
Can be used for specific indications or contraindications to the preferred agent, but the allergy label alone does not establish those indications.
Not a standard IV orthopedic prophylaxis choice in this setting.

questions.prompt: During the case, a critical instrument is dropped onto the floor and there is no sterile replacement available. After decontaminating the instrument for Immediate Use Steam Sterilization (IUSS), what must the circulating nurse include with the instrument in the IUSS rigid container?
options: A Bowie-Dick test
A chemical integrator
A biological indicator and Bowie-Dick test
A chemical integrator and external indicator
questions.explanation: An internal chemical indicator is needed inside the validated IUSS container. External indicators remain outside when applicable. The whole process also requires physical checks, biological monitoring as specified, documented cleaning, and validated cycle instructions.
optionExplanations: Tests air removal in applicable sterilizers; it does not replace the internal load indicator.
Provides the internal chemical monitoring asked for.
Neither a biological test nor an air-removal test substitutes for the required internal CI.
An external indicator belongs outside the container; it is not the additional item to place inside.

questions.prompt: Mr. Roberts has been heavily sedated and arrives in the preoperative holding area accompanied by his wife. What is the best way for the perioperative nurse to verify the surgical procedure and site?
options: Check to ensure that the left femur has been marked by the surgeon, and ask the patient if this is correct; ensure that the consent form has been completed by the patient.
Check unique identifiers, bracelet and consent form, but identification of site is not necessary because fracture is obvious.
Verify with the patient and his wife the surgery and site; check unique identifiers, bracelet, consent form and preoperative record.
Confirm the operative site with the surgeon and anesthesia provider; check unique identifiers, bracelet, preoperative record and consent form.
questions.explanation: A heavily sedated patient may not provide dependable verification. Reconcile identifiers, records, consent, and site with the responsible team; involve the wife and patient as their participation permits. Do not infer the operative side from the injury's appearance.
optionExplanations: Assumes a side not given in the case and relies on the sedated patient.
An obvious injury does not waive site verification.
Family input is valuable, but the option relies on patient confirmation despite heavy sedation and omits responsible-team reconciliation.
Reconciles the responsible team and the objective identification and operative records.

questions.prompt: The perioperative nurse will be assisting the anesthesia provider with Mr. Roberts’ induction. What would be critical for the nurse to consider during this time?
options: Facial fractures, broken teeth, aspiration and difficult intubation
Difficult intubation, nose bleed, abdominal trauma and femoral fracture
Hypotension, hypothermia, femoral fracture and aspiration
Facial fractures, nose bleed, head injuries and abdominal trauma
questions.explanation: Facial trauma, disrupted teeth, aspiration risk, and difficult laryngoscopy all directly affect induction and airway planning. Prepare equipment and assistance before induction.
optionExplanations: Groups the most directly relevant airway hazards.
Includes trauma details but omits aspiration and dental hazards.
Important physiological risks, but does not address the facial and dental airway problems as completely.
Omits the difficult-airway and aspiration considerations central to induction.

questions.prompt: What should the perioperative nurse do to ensure Mr. Roberts’ safe transfer to the operating room table?
options: Reassure the patient, introduce him to the surgical team and assist him to move to the operating room table.
Lock the stretcher in place and use three staff members to help log-roll the patient to the operating room table.
Carefully hold the fractured leg, reassure the patient and ask him to slowly move to the pre-warmed operating room table.
Have adequate personnel to transfer the patient, ensuring that the operating room stretcher and bed are locked in place.
questions.explanation: Use enough trained personnel and appropriate transfer aids, lock both surfaces, protect the injured limb and lines, and coordinate the transfer. The staffing requirement depends on the patient and device.
optionExplanations: A heavily sedated, multiply injured patient cannot be expected to transfer independently.
Locks only one surface and imposes a fixed method and staff count without assessment.
Still relies on unsafe independent movement in this case.
Establishes coordinated assistance and stable transfer surfaces.

questions.prompt: What risk factors might cause a life-threatening situation such as cardiac arrest, stroke (brain attack) or myocardial infarction?
options: Hypotension, cardiac dysrhythmias, massive hemorrhage and stress
Pulmonary embolism, abdominal compartment syndrome, short neck and age
Hypovolemia, possible chest injuries, allergies and a barrel chest
Cardiac dysrhythmias, hypertension, nose bleeds and allergies
questions.explanation: Hemorrhage, hypotension, and dysrhythmias can threaten perfusion and progress to arrest or ischemic injury. Detect deterioration, communicate it, and support the coordinated resuscitation plan.
optionExplanations: Contains the clearest direct hemodynamic threats described by the question.
Includes serious possibilities but mixes them with a nonspecific anatomical feature.
Includes hypovolemia but adds findings that do not establish the stated life-threatening risk.
Nosebleeds and an allergy label are less direct than massive hemorrhage and hypotension here.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Samuels, 88 years old, is being anesthetized for a low anterior bowel resection. After plugging the electrosurgical unit (ESU) into the grounded wall outlet, the circulating nurse notices that the connection port at the back of the machine is frayed and the wires are exposed. This is the only ESU in the hospital not in use or out for repair. Which one of the following sequences of actions should the circulating nurse take?
options: Contact maintenance personnel, tape the wires, proceed with the case and write an incident report.
Inform the nurse-in-charge, inform biomedical engineering, write an incident report and proceed with the case.
Inform the nurse-in-charge, inform the surgeon, remove the ESU from the operating room and call biomedical engineering.
Inform the surgeon, arrange for the ESU to be checked at the end of the day by biomedical engineering and proceed with the case.
questions.explanation: Do not use a unit with exposed wiring. Communicate the equipment problem, remove it from service, and arrange biomedical assessment and a safe alternative before proceeding.
optionExplanations: Tape is not a validated repair for damaged equipment.
Notification and reporting do not make the unit safe to use.
Removes the known hazard and initiates appropriate assessment.
Defers correction while exposing the patient and staff to the hazard.

questions.prompt: After insertion of the laparoscope into the peritoneal cavity, bleeding is observed on the monitor but the source of bleeding is not visible to the surgeon. Which of the following should the scrub nurse anticipate the surgeon will use next?
options: Calibrated metal probe and insulated electrosurgical instruments
Laparotomy instrument set
Electrosurgical instruments and suction tubing
Suction irrigating set and insulated electrosurgical instruments
questions.explanation: Suction and irrigation improve visualization of the bleeding source; compatible insulated electrosurgical instruments may then be needed for hemostasis. Be prepared to convert if bleeding cannot be controlled laparoscopically.
optionExplanations: A probe does not clear the blood obscuring the source.
May be needed if conversion becomes necessary, but that is not yet established.
Includes suction but omits the irrigating equipment useful for restoring visualization.
Supports visualization and subsequent hemostasis through the laparoscopic approach.

questions.prompt: During surgery for a fractured ankle, the surgeon requests that an X-ray be taken. The pretailored disposable drape to cover the X-ray cassette is not available. What should the scrub nurse do?
options: Raise the leg and place the cassette under the drapes.
Place a cassette in a cassette holder and cover with a sterile drape.
Have the radiology technologist place the cassette in a sterile Mayo stand cover.
Call the nurse-in-charge to discuss the product shortage with the surgeon.
questions.explanation: A sterile Mayo stand cover can provide an alternative barrier if it is compatible with the cassette and local procedure. Introduce the nonsterile cassette into the cover without contaminating the outside or field.
optionExplanations: Manipulates the limb and cassette without describing an adequate enclosed barrier.
A loosely draped cassette does not describe protection during movement as well as an enclosing cover.
Provides an enclosing sterile barrier using the stated alternative cover.
Product review is useful later but does not directly provide the needed barrier now.

questions.prompt: A surgeon performing a laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy on a 48-year-old patient completes the abdominal portion. Following completion of the vaginal portion, the surgeon returns to the abdominal area to ensure hemostasis and closure of the abdominal trocar port sites. What should the circulating nurse instruct the surgical team to do?
options: Take no corrective action because the procedure is clean/contaminated.
Regown and reglove the surgeon, and redrape the entire field after completion of the vaginal portion.
Regown and reglove the team on return to the abdomen.
Suggest that the surgeon totally conclude the abdominal work before starting the vaginal portion.
questions.explanation: Returning from the vaginal portion to the cleaner abdominal field requires preventing transfer of contamination, including new sterile gowns and gloves and separation of contaminated instruments according to policy.
optionExplanations: Wound classification does not waive separation of clean and contaminated stages.
May add steps beyond those required for an intact abdominal field and refers only to the surgeon.
Restores the team barriers before returning to the abdominal field.
Suggesting a different operative order does not correct the current transition.

questions.prompt: A 67-year-old female patient is having a brain tumour removed. The surgeon using the air-powered drill to make the burr holes asks the circulating nurse to increase the speed. What should the nurse do first to ensure safe use of this equipment?
options: Increase the pressure setting to attain the desired speed requested by the surgeon.
Check that the accessory is attached securely into the handpiece.
Provide the surgeon with a new burr.
Verify the pressure setting is in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommended limits.
questions.explanation: Verify the permitted pressure range in the manufacturer's instructions before changing a powered drill setting. Check connections and accessories as part of safe equipment use.
optionExplanations: An unverified increase can exceed the device's permitted settings.
Accessory security is important, but does not determine whether the requested increase is permitted.
A new burr does not verify the safe operating pressure.
Checks the requested adjustment against validated operating limits.

questions.prompt: Mr. Elgin, a non-fasting 33-year-old patient, is undergoing an open reduction internal fixation for a comminuted fractured left tibia. When assisting with the administration of his general anesthetic, what should the circulating nurse anticipate?
options: Assist with a rapid sequence induction.
Assist with the insertion of a nasogastric tube.
Hold the endotracheal tube in preparation for intubation.
Place Mr. Elgin in reverse Trendelenburg.
questions.explanation: A non-fasting urgent patient has aspiration risk. Anticipate the anesthesia provider's rapid-sequence airway plan, with preoxygenation, suction, backup airway equipment, and assigned team roles.
optionExplanations: Addresses aspiration risk through the planned induction technique.
A gastric tube alone does not provide a protected airway or replace the induction plan.
This is routine assistance, but omits the specific aspiration-risk preparation.
Positioning alone does not replace the aspiration-risk induction plan.

questions.prompt: Mr. Deere, 63 years old, has just had a right upper lobectomy and has a chest tube to underwater sealed drainage. His blood loss was moderate and was replaced during the procedure with Ringer's lactate. He had a right total hip replacement performed 1 month ago. He was very concerned about his wife preoperatively because she was quite distraught. The circulating nurse is giving the report to the post-anesthesia care unit nurse. In addition to the blood loss, what information is the most important for the circulating nurse to include in the report?
options: Type of fluid replacement
His previous surgery
His concerns about his wife preoperatively
Information about his diagnosis
questions.explanation: Among these choices, the type and amount of replacement fluid directly support assessment of fluid balance and perfusion after blood loss. The complete handoff also includes respiratory status, the chest drain, procedure, and complications.
optionExplanations: Completes the immediate blood-loss and replacement information.
Relevant history, but less directly tied to the immediate fluid-balance issue.
Psychosocial concerns matter, but do not replace the physiological handoff.
Diagnosis is necessary background, but does not complete the described fluid-replacement report.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Patel is under general anesthetic for a left nephrectomy. In addition to a body strap or tape, which devices might the circulating nurse use to prevent possible complications while positioning her in the right lateral position?
options: Kidney elevator and bolsters
Axillary roll and kidney elevator
Headrest and folded sheets
Shoulder brace and arm boards
questions.explanation: An appropriately placed chest support or axillary roll protects the dependent axilla, while kidney-positioning supports provide exposure without excessive pressure. The roll is placed caudal to the axilla, not directly in it.
optionExplanations: Does not explicitly protect the dependent axillary structures.
Addresses the dependent axilla and the kidney-position requirements.
Does not describe the specific support needed to protect the lateral position.
Shoulder braces are not the usual lateral kidney-position solution and can add nerve pressure.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Klein, 62 years old, is scheduled for closure of colostomy. How should the circulating nurse perform the skin prep?
options: Place a towel over the stoma, prep from the stoma site to periphery and then remove the towel.
Start the prep at the stoma site, work outwardly and use a clean sponge each time.
Isolate the stoma with a sponge soaked with prep solution, prep the surrounding area and then prep stoma area.
Pack the stoma with a water-soaked sponge, prep from stoma to periphery and then leave the sponge for removal by the scrub nurse.
questions.explanation: Isolate the stoma while preparing the cleaner surrounding incision area, then prepare the stoma separately. This reduces transfer of organisms from the stoma to the cleaner skin.
optionExplanations: Starts at the more contaminated stoma site.
Carries contamination outward from the stoma.
Follows cleaner-to-more-contaminated preparation.
Starts at the stoma and leaves an item in place without the indicated separate preparation.

questions.prompt: Akira, 10 years old, is scheduled for strabismus surgery. During preoperative assessment, Akira tells the circulating nurse that she is allergic to avocados and bananas. What is the priority nursing action for the circulating nurse?
options: Check that the allergies are documented and that Akira is wearing an allergy band.
Verify these allergies with Akira’s parents.
Inform the surgical team that Akira may have a latex allergy.
Communicate the allergies to the post-anesthesia care unit team.
questions.explanation: Banana and avocado reactions can signal latex-fruit cross-reactivity. Alert the team to possible latex sensitivity and assess the history so precautions can be planned before exposure.
optionExplanations: Documentation is needed, but communicating the additional latex concern is the priority.
Confirmation is useful, but does not replace prompt team communication.
Identifies the relevant perioperative exposure risk.

questions.prompt: While setting up the back table, the perioperative scrub nurse observes that the double basin set does not have an internal chemical integrator. What would be the best practice to ensure that aseptic technique is followed?

Inform the circulating nurse that she will need a new double basin set, and remove gloves and anything else that may have come in contact with the double basin.
Continue setting up the back table since the external indicator tape changed colour and therefore there is no concern.

optionExplanations: Replacing the set is necessary, but this option omits assessment of contacted gloves and field items.

To ensure that all implants will be sterile following processing
To ensure that all air has been removed from the autoclave before sterilization
To ensure that the sterilizer has met the parameters necessary for sterilization

Overstates assurance for every implant and ignores the full release process.

cases.REC-CASE-1: Donna, the circulating nurse, is admitting 16-year-old Nina to the operating room to have a laparoscopic appendectomy. Nina is allergic to shellfish, dust and recently reacted to penicillin.

cases.REC-CASE-4: Chad, 16 years old, is brought to the operating room suite for open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a fractured right femur and ORIF of his left arm sustained in a motor vehicle collision. recording-priority.title: Selecting the best nursing action
recording-priority.text: Read the exact task: first action, anticipated equipment, risk factor, or handoff priority. Use the case findings to identify the immediate problem, then choose the action that addresses it within the nurse’s role. An option can be true in general yet less appropriate at that point. Do not invent findings that the stem does not supply.

recording-airway.title: Airway problems around anesthesia
recording-airway.text: Induction and emergence are vulnerable phases. Distinguish obstruction, difficult intubation, aspiration risk, and residual weakness. Nursing preparation includes suction, appropriate airway equipment, monitoring, and coordinated assistance. Laryngospasm is reflex glottic closure; oxygenation and airway maneuvers are urgent, with medication escalation led by the anesthesia provider.

recording-reversal.title: Neuromuscular blockade and reversal
recording-reversal.text: A neuromuscular blocker produces paralysis, not hypnosis or analgesia. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase to help reverse suitable nondepolarizing blockade; quantitative monitoring guides timing and recovery. Verify the injectable formulation and associated antimuscarinic medication. A sedative such as propofol does not reverse paralysis.

recording-last.title: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity
recording-last.text: Systemic local anesthetic exposure can produce neurological symptoms, seizures, and cardiovascular collapse. Stop further exposure, summon help, and support airway and oxygenation. Activate the local LAST protocol and obtain the rescue kit, including lipid emulsion. The ASRA checklist differs from routine cardiac-arrest drug practice.

recording-allergy.title: Allergy assessment and perioperative exposures
recording-allergy.text: Identify the substance, reaction, timing, severity, and previous safe exposures. Latex sensitivity may be suggested by reactions to banana or avocado. A drug-allergy label does not identify the mechanism or automatically rule out every related drug. Communicate the history before exposure and prepare the indicated precautions and response.

recording-position.title: Individualized positioning
recording-position.text: Assess comfortable movement, joint disease, prostheses, amputations, body habitus, and skin before anesthesia. Protect ventilation, circulation, nerves, and pressure areas. In lithotomy, coordinate movement of both legs; in prone, avoid chest and abdominal compression; in lateral, protect the dependent axilla. Recheck after movement.

recording-sterile.title: A barrier breach versus a protected delay
recording-sterile.text: A torn, wet, or uncertain barrier needs assessment and immediate correction. Covering cannot sterilize contaminated supplies. An intact field during a delay is different: ORNAC permits proper covering in specified circumstances while continuous monitoring continues. If monitoring or sterility cannot be assured, replace or reprocess affected supplies.

recording-iuss.title: IUSS and sterility assurance
recording-iuss.text: IUSS is reserved for urgent, unplanned needs. Thorough cleaning, validated cycles and containers, physical checks, internal chemical indicators, daily biological testing, and traceability still apply. A chemical color change or a single negative BI is not an absolute guarantee for every item. Transfer in the validated closed container and use promptly.

recording-energy.title: Electrosurgery and the return pathway
recording-energy.text: Monopolar energy requires a suitable return electrode on clean, dry, well-perfused tissue near the operative site. Avoid scarred or compromised skin, prostheses, and unsuitable current paths. Verify the plan for implanted electronic devices. Inspect contact and skin, follow device instructions, and remove malfunctioning equipment from service.

recording-fire.title: Fire prevention and response
recording-fire.text: The fire triad consists of fuel, ignition, and an oxidizer. Prevent prep pooling, remove wet absorbent material, allow appropriate drying, and control energy devices and oxygen through team communication. During a fire, protect the patient and carry out assigned immediate control actions; safety reporting follows the emergency response.

recording-counts.title: Counts and discrepancy management
recording-counts.text: Both nurses verify countable items visually and audibly. Small incisions and few sharps do not eliminate the count or safe-containment requirements. Communicate a missing item promptly, recount and search systematically, and follow the retained-item protocol for unresolved or omitted counts. An emergency needs coordinated roles and documentation.

recording-incident.title: Injury recognition, reporting, and handoff
recording-incident.text: Assess and treat the patient first. Preserve relevant equipment and evidence, document objective clinical findings and care in the patient record, communicate follow-up needs, and complete the separate organizational safety report. Avoid attributing an unexplained injury to a patient characteristic or omitting it because it seems minor.
